the_refusal_is_a_rule_defect_not_a_namin.description: The gate printed both a REFUSE and an 'Owed' replacement name, which invites typing the replacement in. Whether that is a genuine naming verdict was checked at the source by calling the builder directly on both names, instead of reading the gate's message as authoritative.
the_refusal_is_a_rule_defect_not_a_namin.expected_landed: If the policy name were simply non-conformant, grade() would RETURN a verdict plus a canonical name, and the owed name would be the canon's answer.
the_refusal_is_a_rule_defect_not_a_namin.expected_not_landed: If it is a rule or registry defect, grade() cannot reach a verdict at all and raises.
the_refusal_is_a_rule_defect_not_a_namin.observed: The defect reading. opal_naming.grade('restricted-prefix-get-put-list','IAM_POLICY') RAISES RaiseDefect('R1.f: restricted is in no vocabulary; no registry row resolves it') -- no verdict is returned -- while the sibling opal_naming.grade('cloudops-cot-restricted-breakglass-role','IAM_ROLE') returns ('CONFORMANT', ...) normally. This matches the gate's own parenthetical ('a rule or registry defect, not a naming verdict') and is why the owed name was NOT adopted. Independently: the owed name cloudops-49f-restricted-breakglass-policy carries the 49f firm token on a policy granting only on opal-data-cottonwood's commonwealth/cottonwood/bronze/crm/ prefix, while the same gate blessed the sibling role as cloudops-cot- -- so typing it in would commit a cross-firm mislabel on an IAM object.
